Theme

Body, health & movement

depression noun

of mind

also low spirits, dejection, despondency, melancholy, depressive

classical

Cic. Att. 9.10.1

aegritūdō, aegritūdinis f.

noun, third declension

distress, depression, grief

Cicero’s word for the lasting distress of mind that his philosophy treats as an illness of the soul (Tusc. 3–4), and the nearest classical word for depression; it is also grief and sorrow in general. Of the body, illness, only after Augustus (Lewis & Short).

Other words

  • animī dēmissiō — dejection, low spirits

    also used · classical · Cic. Tusc. 3.14 (Lewis & Short)

  • contractiō animī — dejection, depression

    also used · classical · Cic. Tusc. 4.66 (Lewis & Short); Traupman 151

    Cicero’s contrast to effūsiō animī in joy: the shrinking of the mind in pain.

  • abjectiō animī — dejection, despondency

    also used · classical · Cic. Pis. 88 (Lewis & Short); Traupman 303

  • melancholicus, melancholica, melancholicum — melancholic, depressive

    also used · classical · Cic. Tusc. 1.80 (Lewis & Short); M-O s.v. depressed

    Literally having black bile; Cicero cites it from Aristotle.

Examples

  • sed cum mē aegritūdō nōn sōlum somnō prīvāret vērum nē vigilāre quidem sine summō dolōre paterētur

    but since my distress not only robbed me of sleep but would not even let me be awake without the greatest painCic. Att. 9.10.1

  • Aristotelēs quidem ait omnēs ingeniōsōs melancholicōs esse

    Aristotle indeed says that all men of genius are melancholicCic. Tusc. 1.80 (Lewis & Short)

See also sadness, sad, disease.
